Whatever Happens to Bonds, Stocks Win
 
Plus, Brent crude climbs and chip stocks are mixed
 
By Heard on the Street Staff
 
 
DIMITAR DILKOFF/AGENCE FRANCE-PRESSE/GETTY IMAGES
 

This is an edition of the Markets P.M. newsletter, a recap of the day’s most important markets moves, delivered after the closing bell. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

What Happened in Markets Today

 

Stocks hit new records as bond yields eased a bit. Yields down, stocks win. Yields up, stocks win. That’s the story of the week so far. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite both ended at new record closing levels on Tuesday. The S&P 500 added 0.6%, and the Nasdaq Composite rose 0.5%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 253 points, or 0.5%.

 

Treasury yields eased from recent highs. Ten-year Treasury yields declined to just under 5.27% by session’s end, after hitting their highest levels since 2002 on Monday. The U.S. Treasury will test the market on Wednesday with a 10-year note auction.

 

Rising global bond yields are still making investors nervous. French government bonds have been under pressure lately, with concerns about the country’s fiscal outlook. France’s 10-year borrowing cost has risen toward 5%. Those yields eased a bit on Tuesday, along with U.S. Treasury and German Bunds.

 

Oil prices climbed slightly. Brent crude moved back from the $100 threshold, edging 0.3% higher to $100.58 a barrel. Shipments are picking up as exporters find new routes, but there remain threats of attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.

 

Chip stocks were mixed. Seagate Technology fell more than 9%, following a report that it was facing the prospect of a bidding contest to acquire a component maker. Western Digital also fell sharply, by almost 7%. Overall, however, the PHLX Semiconductor index eked out a gain for the day. Marvell Technology gained almost 6% after an investor-day presentation with a big revenue target.

One Big Story

 
 
JASON HENRY FOR WSJ
 

Oura’s glossy smart ring is everywhere these days: in high-profile TV ad campaigns and on the fingers of plenty of people.

 

Yet when Oura tried to go public late last month, it couldn’t find enough buyers at its proposed price and shelved the listing. The company blamed jittery markets, despite major stock indexes being near record highs, and said it could afford to pick its moment.

 

Surging Treasury yields were certainly part of the problem. The bigger challenge, though, was a mismatch between how Oura sees itself and how prospective investors saw it.
